summary: Defines a Diameter application and command codes that allow a peer's capabilities to be updated dynamically while the connection stays open. This avoids tearing down a connection just to change what a peer supports. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally if you learn a new skill, you would have to leave the room to tell everyone. This lets you announce it right there without leaving the conversation.

questions: change diameter peer capabilities without reconnecting
what is the diameter capabilities update application
how to update diameter capabilities without reconnecting
subtitle: A Diameter application that lets two peers update their advertised capabilities without tearing down the connection.

tldr.problem: Diameter peers exchange capabilities only once, when a transport connection starts, so a change such as a software update forces the connection and all its user sessions to be torn down and restarted.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6737 defines the Capabilities Update application (Application-Id 10) with a Capabilities-Update-Request and Capabilities-Update-Answer pair (Command Code 328) that peers send over the open connection.
tldr.outcome: Peers can refresh most capabilities in place. Changing the security mechanism is not allowed this way, and the connection MUST be restarted in that case.

facts.label: Request flag
facts.value: R bit set on CUR, cleared on CUA

today: RFC 6737 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2012. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the Diameter base protocol in RFC 6733.

sections.title: The Problem With One-Time Capabilities Exchange
sections.content:
Capabilities exchange is an important part of the Diameter base protocol, RFC 6733. Peers swap identities and capabilities such as the protocol version number, supported Diameter applications and security mechanisms. As defined in RFC 3588, this happens only once, when a transport connection between a pair of peers begins.

So if a peer's capabilities change, for example after a software update, the existing connections must be torn down along with all their user sessions and restarted before the new capabilities can be advertised. This document avoids that by defining a new application for updating a subset of capabilities over an existing connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine you could only tell your friends what games you own when you first walk in. To announce a new game you would have to leave and come back in. This memo lets you just say it.

sections.title: What Cannot Be Updated
sections.content: Because the application runs over an already open transport connection, changing some capabilities is prohibited. Specifically, the security mechanism in use cannot be modified this way. If the security method between a pair of peers changes, the affected connection MUST be restarted.
sections.plainLanguage: You can announce new skills while talking, but if you want to switch to a secret code, you have to start the conversation over.

sections.title: Advertising Support
sections.content:
The application uses Diameter Application-Id 10. A node that conforms to this specification MUST advertise support by putting the value 10 in the Auth-Application-Id of its Capabilities-Exchange-Request (CER) and Capabilities-Exchange-Answer (CEA) commands from RFC 6733.

A node only sends a given command to peers that advertised support for the application that defines it. It must cache the supported applications so that unrecognized commands and Attribute-Value Pairs (AVPs) are not sent to a peer needlessly.
sections.plainLanguage: When two peers first meet, each says "I know the capabilities-update trick" by listing the number 10. Only then do they use it with each other.

sections.title: How an Update Works
sections.content:
When the capabilities of a conforming node change, it MUST notify every node that has an open transport connection to it and has also advertised support for this application. The notice is a Capabilities-Update-Request (CUR).

The receiver works out the common applications by intersecting its own supported Application Ids with all the Application-Id AVPs in the CUR (Auth-Application-Id, Acct-Application-Id and Vendor-Specific-Application-Id). The Vendor-Id inside the Vendor-Specific-Application-Id MUST NOT be used in this computation.

If there are no applications in common, the receiver MUST return a Capabilities-Update-Answer (CUA) with Result-Code set to DIAMETER_NO_COMMON_APPLICATION and SHOULD disconnect the transport connection. If active sessions use the connection, peers MAY delay disconnecting until the sessions can be redirected or gracefully terminated. A CUA from a peer that advertises itself as a relay MUST be treated as meaning there are common applications.
sections.plainLanguage: When something changes, you tell each friend who knows the trick. They check which games you both still have. If you share none, they politely end the chat.

sections.title: No Proxying and Delivery Failures
sections.content:
Like CER and CEA, the CUR and CUA messages MUST NOT be proxied, redirected or relayed. Even so, an upstream agent might receive a message for which no peer is available to handle the application for that Command Code, for example because peers are too busy or down. In that case the E bit MUST be set in the answer, with Result-Code set to DIAMETER_UNABLE_TO_DELIVER, so the downstream peer can act, for instance by re-routing requests to an alternate peer.

Upon detection of a transport failure, a CUR MUST NOT be sent to an alternate peer.
sections.plainLanguage: This message is only for the two friends talking directly, so nobody may pass it along. If a middleman cannot reach anyone, it says so and the sender can try another route for normal requests.

sections.title: The CUR and CUA Messages
sections.content:
Both messages use Command Code 328. The Capabilities-Update-Request has the R bit set. It requires Origin-Host, Origin-Realm, Vendor-Id and Product-Name, and at least one Host-IP-Address. It may also carry Origin-State-Id, Supported-Vendor-Id, the application id AVPs, Firmware-Revision and further AVPs.

When Diameter runs over SCTP, which lets connections span multiple interfaces and IP addresses, the CUR MUST contain one Host-IP-Address AVP for each IP address that may be used locally when sending Diameter messages.

The Capabilities-Update-Answer has the R bit cleared and carries Origin-Host, Origin-Realm and Result-Code, with optional Error-Message. All conforming implementations MUST support both commands.
sections.plainLanguage: The request is a short note listing who you are and what you can do now. The answer is a short reply saying whether that worked.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The security considerations of the Diameter base protocol, RFC 6733, also apply to this document.

IANA assigned the value 10 (Diameter Capabilities Update) from the Application Identifiers namespace and the value 328 (CUR/CUA) from the Command Codes namespace.
sections.plainLanguage: The same safety rules as ordinary Diameter apply. The two numbers 10 and 328 were officially reserved for this feature.

items.title: No relaying
items.text: CUR and CUA MUST NOT be proxied, redirected or relayed.

items.title: Security changes
items.text: Changing the security mechanism requires restarting the connection.
